(Forty-five verses, Meccan)

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿All praise belongs to God, Originator of the heavens and the earth, Who made the angels messengers﴾

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿All praise belongs to God, Originator of the heavens and the earth, Who made the angels messengers﴾. We have already mentioned in what came before that praise (al-hamd) is for a blessing in most cases. The blessings of God are of two kinds: immediate (ajilah) and deferred (ajilah's counterpart, ājilah, the afterlife). The immediate blessing is existence and continuance, and the deferred blessing is likewise: origination once and preservation another time. God's words, ﴿All praise belongs to God, who created the heavens and the earth and made the darknesses and the light﴾ [al-An'am: 1], point to the immediate blessing, which is origination. We derived this from His words, ﴿It is He who created you from clay, then decreed a term﴾ [al-An'am: 2]. His words in al-Kahf, ﴿All praise belongs to God, who sent down the Book upon His servant﴾ [al-Kahf: 1], point to the immediate blessing, which is preservation, for survival and well-being come through the Law (al-shar') and the Book. Without it, disputes and quarrels would arise among people and they would not be judged between, which would lead to killing and mutual destruction. So the sending down of the Book is a blessing on which immediate survival depends. In His words in Surat Saba': ﴿All praise belongs to God, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth, and to Him belongs praise in the Hereafter﴾ [Saba': 1], there is a reference to the blessing of the second origination through the Gathering (al-hashr). We derived this from His words, ﴿He knows what enters into the earth﴾ [Saba': 2], which refers to bodies, ﴿and what emerges from it and what descends from the sky﴾ [Saba': 2], which refers to spirits, ﴿and what ascends into it﴾ [Saba': 2]. Also His words about the disbelievers: ﴿Those who disbelieved said, "The Hour will not come to us." Say, "Yes, by my Lord"﴾ [Saba': 3]. Here, praise points to the blessing of survival in the Hereafter. This is indicated by His words, ﴿Who made the angels messengers﴾, meaning He makes them messengers who receive God's servants, as He said, ﴿and the angels will receive them﴾ [al-Anbiya': 103].

On this basis, His words ﴿Originator of the heavens﴾ may have two meanings. The first: its meaning is "its Innovator (mubdi')," as is reported from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: ﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾ means "the One who splits them," for the spirits descend from the sky and the bodies emerge from the earth. This is indicated by His words, ﴿Who made the angels messengers﴾, for on that Day the angels will be messengers. On this basis, the beginning of this surah is connected to the end of what preceded it, because His words, "as was done with their likes" (Saba': 54), explain the cutting off of hope for one who was in doubtful suspicion, and his certainty that there is no acceptance of his repentance and no benefit in his saying "I believe." As He said about them: ﴿They said, "We believe in Him." But how could they reach it from a place far away?﴾ [Saba': 52]. When He mentioned their state, He explained the state of the one who is certain, gave him good news of the sending of the angels to them as bringers of good tidings, and explained that He opens for them the gates of mercy.

﴿Possessors of wings, two, three, or four. He adds to creation what He wills. Indeed, God is Able over all things﴾. ﴿Whatever mercy God opens for people, none can withhold; and whatever He withholds, none can release after Him﴾. God's words ﴿Possessors of wings, two, three, or four﴾: the least that a winged being can have is two wings, and what follows is addition. Some said regarding this that "wing" is an indication of direction. Its explanation is that God, Exalted, has nothing above Him, and everything is under His power and blessing. The angels have a direction toward God from which they take His blessings and give them to those below them, from what they have taken, by God's permission, as He said, ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit brought it down upon your heart﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 193–194], and His words, ﴿Taught him by one mighty in power﴾ [al-Najm: 5], and He said about them, ﴿And those who arrange (the affair) by command﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 5]. These are two wings. Among them are those who do the good they do through an intermediary, and among them are those who do it without an intermediary. The one who acts through an intermediary has three directions, and some have four directions or more. The apparent meaning is what we mentioned first, and it is what the exegetes (al-mufassirun) have agreed upon.

God's words ﴿He adds to creation what He wills﴾: some of the exegetes restricted it and said: it means a beautiful face; others said: a beautiful voice; others said: every praiseworthy attribute. The better view is that it be generalized, and it is said: God, Exalted, is Powerful and Perfect and does what He wills, so He increases what He wills and decreases what He wills.

God's words ﴿Indeed, God is Able over all things﴾ confirm His words ﴿He adds to creation what He wills﴾.

Then God, Exalted, said: ﴿Whatever mercy God opens for people, none can withhold; and whatever He withholds, none can release after Him﴾.

When He explained His perfect power, He mentioned the explanation of the effectiveness of His will and the execution of His command. He said: "Whatever God opens for people" meaning: if He shows mercy, no one can prevent it; and if He does not show mercy, no one can move Him to it. In the verse there is evidence that His mercy precedes His wrath, in several respects:

First: the precedence, in that He placed the explanation of the opening of the gates of mercy first in the mention, and although this is weak, it is still one of the aspects of excellence.

Second: He made the pronoun feminine in the first clause, saying ﴿Whatever mercy God opens for people, none can withhold it﴾. Grammatically it would be permissible to say "to it" with the pronoun referring to "what" (ma), but God said ﴿it﴾ (la-ha) to make known that what is opened is the gates of mercy, and none can withhold His mercy, so it is a means of reaching whomever He has mercy upon. And at the withholding He said ﴿whatever He withholds, none can release after Him﴾ with the masculine form, and did not say "for them" (lahuma). Thus He did not state explicitly that there is no one who releases mercy; rather He mentioned it in a wording that allows the one who does not release to be other than mercy, for God's words ﴿whatever He withholds﴾ are general without explanation or specification, unlike His words ﴿Whatever mercy God opens for people﴾, which is specified and clarified.

Third: His words ﴿after Him﴾, meaning after God. Here He made an exception and said: none releases it except God, so it was revealed as "releasing it." At the withholding He said: none can withhold it, and did not say "other than God," because when mercy comes it is not lifted, for whoever God has mercy upon in the Hereafter, He does not punish afterward, neither He nor anyone else. And whoever God punishes, God may then have mercy on him after the punishment, like the sinners among the people of faith.

Then God Most High said: ﴿And He is the All-Mighty﴾, that is, of perfect power, ﴿the All-Wise﴾, that is, of perfect knowledge.

﴿O mankind, remember the favour of God upon you﴾

When He had stated that all praise belongs to God, and had mentioned some aspects of the favour that merits praise in detail, He mentioned His favours in summary, saying: ﴿Remember the favour of God﴾. Despite their multitude, they are confined to two kinds: the favour of origination (ni'mat al-ijad) and the favour of sustenance (ni'mat al-ibqa').

God Most High said: ﴿Is there any creator other than God?﴾, pointing to the favour of origination at the beginning.

And God Most High said: ﴿Who provides for you from the heaven and the earth﴾, pointing to the favour of sustaining existence through provision until its end.

Then He stated that ﴿there is no god but Him﴾, in view of His greatness, since He is All-Mighty, All-Wise, capable of everything, the Omnipotent whose will is executed in everything, and there is none like Him, and no one is worthy of worship in His essence other than Him; and in view of His favour, since there is no creator other than Him and no provider except Him.

Then God Most High said: ﴿How then are you turned away?﴾, that is, how are you diverted from this manifest truth? How then do you associate with Him the carved idols something that is hewn, with the One who possesses the dominion (malakut)?

Then, having stated the first foundation, which is monotheism (tawhid), He mentioned the second foundation, which is prophethood (risalah), saying: ﴿And if they deny you, messengers before you were denied﴾.

Then He stated in summary that the one who denies is subject to punishment, and the one who is denied is due reward, by His saying: ﴿And to God all matters are returned﴾. Then He stated the third foundation, which is the Resurrection (hashr).

He said: ﴿O mankind, indeed the promise of God is true, so let not the worldly life deceive you, and let not the Deceiver deceive you concerning God﴾, that is, Satan. We have already mentioned the subtle meaning in it in the tafsir of Surat Luqman, and we repeat it here, so we say: The responsible person may be weak in mind, of little intellect and foolish judgment, so he is deceived by the slightest thing. He may be above that, so he is not deceived by it, but when a deceiver comes to him, adorns that thing for him, makes its corruptions seem light to him, and shows him its benefits, he is deceived because of the pleasure in it, together with what is added by that deceiver's calling him to it. He may be strong of heart and abundant in intellect, so he is neither deceived nor made to be deceived. God Most High said: ﴿So let not the worldly life deceive you﴾, pointing to the first level, and He said: ﴿Nor let the Deceiver deceive you concerning God﴾, pointing to the second, so that one may be in the third level, which is the highest, so he is neither deceived nor made to be deceived.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿He only invites his party that they may be among the companions of the Blaze﴾. This points to a subtle meaning, namely that whoever has an enemy has two ways regarding his matter:

The first: that he opposes him in return for his opposition.

The second: that he removes his enmity by pleasing him. When God, exalted is He, said ﴿Indeed, Satan is an enemy to you﴾, He commanded them to be hostile to him and indicated that the way is nothing but this. As for the other way, which is appeasement, there is no benefit in it, because if you appease him and follow him, he will lead you only to the Blaze.

Know that whoever knows that he has an enemy from whom there is no escape, and is certain of this, will stand firm before him and be patient in fighting him, and patience with him brings victory. Likewise, Satan: a person cannot flee from him, for he is always with him and keeps following him, unless he stands against him and defeats him. So the defeat of Satan is by the resolve of the person. The way is steadfastness upon the right path and reliance upon worship.

Then God explained the condition of his party and the condition of the party of God, saying:

﴿Those who disbelieve, for them is a severe punishment﴾. The one who opposes Satan, although in the present he is in a apparent punishment that is not severe, and the intelligent person chooses a small, temporary punishment to avert a severe, everlasting punishment. Do you not see that when a person encounters on his path a thorn and a fire, and has no choice but one of the two, he steps over the thorn and does not enter the fire? The ratio of the fire of this world to the fire of the Hereafter is less than the ratio of the thorn to the immediate fire.

And God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And those who believe and do righteous deeds, for them is forgiveness and a great reward﴾. Its explanation has been mentioned many times, and it was made clear that faith is met with forgiveness, so no believer will be eternally abiding in the Fire, and righteous deeds are met with a great reward.

Then God Most High said: ﴿Is he, to whom the evil of his deeds has been made attractive so that he sees it as good, [equal to one who does right]? Indeed, God lets go astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills. So do not let yourself expire in regret over them. Indeed, God is Knowing of what they do.﴾

Meaning: the one who does evil is not like the one who does righteousness, as He said after this, in verses later, ﴿Nor are the blind and the seeing alike, nor the darknesses and the light﴾. It has a connection to what precedes it, in that when God Most High explained the state of the evildoer who is a disbeliever and the doer of good who is a believer, and no one admits to doing evil except a few, the disbeliever would say: "The one who will receive the severe punishment is the one who follows Satan, and he is Muhammad and his people, whom the jinn have enticed and who followed them. And the one who will receive the great reward is us, who persist in what our fathers were upon." So God Most High said: "You are not like that, for the doer of good is different, and the one for whom evil deeds have been made attractive, so that he sees them as good, is different. Rather, those for whom evil has been made attractive are other than the one who does evil and knows that he is an evildoer. For the ignorant one who knows his ignorance, and the evildoer who knows the badness of his deed, returns and repents, whereas the one who does not know persists in sins. The evildoer who knows has the attribute of blame for evildoing and the attribute of praise for knowledge. The evildoer who sees his evildoing as good has two attributes of blame: evildoing and ignorance." Then He explained that all of it is by the will of God, and said: ﴿Indeed, God lets go astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills﴾. That is because people, as individuals, are equal in reality, and evildoing and doing good, and bad deeds and good deeds, are distinguished from one another; when some recognize them and others do not, that is not by their own independence, so there must be reliance on the will of God.

Then He consoled the Messenger of God (ﷺ) when he grieved over their persistence after he had brought them every clear sign and manifest proof, and He said: ﴿So do not let yourself expire in regret over them﴾, as God Most High said: ﴿Perhaps you would destroy yourself with grief over their traces﴾ [al-Kahf: 6].

Then He explained that if his grief is because of their going astray, then God is Knowing of them and of what they do; if He willed their faith and their goodness, He would have prevented them from going astray and turned them back from misguiding others. And if his grief is because of the harm they inflict upon him, then God is Knowing of their act and will recompense them for what they do.

Then he returned to the exposition, saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And it is Allah who sends the winds, so they stir up clouds, and We drive them to a dead land and bring the earth to life thereby after its death. Thus is the resurrection.﴾

The blowing of the winds is a clear proof of the Chooser (al-Fa'il al-Mukhtar), the agent who acts by choice. This is because air may be still or may move, and when it moves it may move to the right or to the left. In its various movements it may produce clouds or it may not. These differences are evidence of a Subduer who directs, a Regulator who governs, and an Ordainer who determines. The verse contains several points (masa'il, sing. mas'alah, a point of discussion):

The first point: He said, ﴿Allah who sent﴾ in the past tense, and He said, ﴿so they stir up clouds﴾ in the present-future form. This is because when He attributed the act of sending to Allah, and what Allah does occurs by His saying "Be," it does not remain in non-existence, neither as a time nor as a part of time. Therefore He did not use the future tense, because its occurrence is certain and its coming into being is swift, as though it had already happened and as though He had finished with everything. He had determined the sending at known times to specified places, and the determining is like the sending itself. As for the stirring up, He attributed it to the wind, which occurs over a period of time, so He said ﴿stirs up﴾, meaning in its present state.

The second point: He said ﴿sent﴾ attributing the verb to the third person (absent), and He said ﴿We drove him﴾ attributing the verb to the first person (speaker), and likewise in His saying ﴿so We brought to life﴾. This is because at the beginning He made Himself known through one of the acts, which is sending. Then, once He had been recognized, He said, in effect: "I am the One you have come to know; I drove the clouds and I gave life to the earth." So the first mention was an introduction through a marvelous act, and the second was a reminder of blessing, since the perfection of the blessing of the winds and clouds lies in their driving and in giving life. His saying "We drove him and brought to life" in the past tense supports what we have mentioned about the difference between His saying ﴿sent﴾ and His saying ﴿stirs up﴾.

The third point: What is the basis of the comparison in His saying ﴿Thus is the resurrection﴾? There are several views:

The first: when the dead earth accepted the life suited to it, likewise the limbs accept life.

The second: just as the wind gathers the pieces of cloud, likewise the parts of the limbs and the scattered components of things are gathered together.

The third: just as We drive the wind and the cloud to the dead land, We drive the spirit and life to the dead body.

The fourth point: What is the wisdom in choosing this verse from among the verses, given that Allah has, in everything, a sign (ayah, a sign or evidence) indicating that He is one? We say: when Allah mentioned that He is the Originator of the heavens and the earth, and mentioned among the heavenly matters the spirits and their sending by His saying ﴿Who made the angels messengers﴾, He mentioned among the earthly matters the winds and their sending by His saying ﴿And it is Allah who sent the winds﴾.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Whoever desires honor—to God belongs all honor. To Him ascends the good word, and the righteous deed raises it. As for those who plot evil deeds, for them is a severe punishment, and the plotting of those will perish.﴾

When He had explained the proof of faith, He alluded to what was preventing the unbelievers from it, namely the apparent honor which they imagined for themselves, on the grounds that they were not under the obedience of anyone and had no one to command or forbid them. So they would carve idols and say, "These are our gods." Then they would carry them along with themselves. And what honor is greater than being in the company of the one worshipped? They were seeking honor, which is the refusal to humble oneself before the Messenger and the refusal to follow him. So He said: If you seek honor through this disbelief in reality, then it all belongs to God, and whoever humbles himself before Him is the mighty one, and whoever exalts himself against Him is the humiliated one. And in the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: He said in this verse, ﴿to God belongs all honor﴾, and He said in another verse, ﴿Honor belongs to God, to His Messenger, and to the believers﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 8]. So His saying ﴿all﴾ indicates that there is no honor for anyone other than Him. We say: His saying ﴿to God belongs honor﴾ means in reality and essentially; His saying ﴿to His Messenger﴾ means through the mediation of closeness to the Mighty, who is God; and ﴿to the believers﴾ means through their closeness to the Mighty by means of God, who is the Messenger. This is because the honor of the believers is through the Prophet ﷺ. Do you not see His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If you love God, then follow me, and God will love you﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 31].

The second issue: His saying ﴿To Him ascends the good word﴾ is a confirmation of the explanation of honor. This is because the unbelievers used to say, "We do not worship one whom we do not see and before whom we do not appear, because distance from the king is abasement." So God, exalted is He, said: If you cannot reach Him, He hears your speech and accepts the good word. Whoever accepts His word and ascends to Him is mighty, and whoever rejects His word to His face is humiliated. As for these idols, the humiliated cannot be distinguished from the mighty in their presence, since they have no knowledge; everyone touches them. Likewise, He sees your deeds: whoever does a righteous deed, He raises it to Himself, and whoever does an evil deed, He returns it upon him. So the mighty is the one whose deed is done for His sake, and the humiliated is the one whose deed is repelled in His face. As for these idols, they know nothing, so no one is raised in their presence, nor is anyone humbled; there is no honor in them, but rather abasement upon them. This is because the abasement of the lord is abasement for the servant. And whoever has as his worshipped one, his lord and his god, a stone or wood, what will he himself be?

The third issue: regarding His saying ﴿To Him ascends the good word﴾ there are several views:

The first: the statement "There is no god but God" is the good word.

The second: "Glory be to God," "Praise be to God," "There is no god but God," and "God is greatest" are good.

The third: these four phrases and a fifth, which is "Blessed is God." The preferred view is that every speech that is a remembrance of God or is for God, such as counsel and knowledge, ascends to Him.

The fourth issue: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and the righteous deed raises it﴾, and regarding the pronoun there are two possibilities:

The first: it refers to the good word; that is, the righteous deed is that which the good word raises. It is reported in a report: "God does not accept a statement without a deed."

The second: it refers to the righteous deed. In this case, regarding the agent who raises there are two possibilities:

The first: the good word raises the righteous deed. This is supported by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whoever does righteousness﴾ (al-Nahl: 97) ﴿male or female while being a believer﴾.

The second: the one who raises is God, exalted is He.

The fifth issue: What is the reason for giving preference to the speech over the deed according to the second view, since the speech ascends by itself while the deed is raised by something else? We say: speech is noble, for the distinction of man over every animal is by speech. Therefore He, exalted is He, said: ﴿We have honored the children of Adam﴾ (al-Isra': 70), meaning by the speaking soul. Deeds are movement and stillness, in which man and others share. The noble one, when he reaches the door of the king, is not prevented, while the one below him does not find the way except upon request. This is indicated by the fact that if the unbeliever speaks the word of testimony sincerely, he is safe from the punishment of this world and the next; and if it is merely outward, he is safe in his person, blood, family, and sanctuary in this world. This is not so for deeds of the limbs. We have mentioned this in the commentary on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ (al-Nisa': 57).

Another view: the heart is the origin, and what indicates this has already been mentioned. The Prophet ﷺ said: ("Indeed, in the body there is a piece of flesh; if it is sound, the whole body is sound, and if it is corrupt, the whole body is corrupt. Indeed, it is the heart.") What is in the heart does not appear except through the tongue, and what is in the tongue is not shown to be truthful except through action. Do you not see that a person does not speak a word except from the heart? As for action, it may occur not from the heart, like fiddling with the beard. Also, the sleeper is never free of some action of movement and turning, yet for the most part he does not speak in his sleep except rarely. Because, as we have mentioned, speech is of the heart and this is not so for deeds. So speech is more noble.

The sixth issue: al-Zamakhshari said: "The verb makr does not take a direct object; so by what is al-sayyi'at (the evil things) in the accusative? He said its meaning is: those who plot evil plots, so it is an adjective of a deleted verbal noun." It may be said that makr is used as deed is used, so it takes its object as it does, just as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Those who do evil deeds﴾ (al-'Ankabut: 7). ﴿And those who plot evil deeds﴾ may bear what we have mentioned: that al-sayyi'at is an adjective of a deleted verbal noun, whose estimate is: those who do the evil deeds. In this case, this is in contrast to His saying: ﴿and the righteous deed raises it﴾, indicating its persistence and elevation. ﴿And the plotting of those﴾, that is, the evil deed, ﴿will perish﴾, indicating its annihilation.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And Allah created you from dust, then from a drop of semen, then He made you into pairs. No female conceives or gives birth except with His knowledge. And no one is granted long life or has his life shortened except that it is in a Book. Indeed, that is easy for Allah.﴾

We have mentioned many times that the proofs, despite their abundance and their not being confined to a fixed number, are restricted to two types: the proofs of the horizons (al-afaq) and the proofs of the selves (al-anfus), as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿We will show them Our signs in the horizons and within themselves﴾ [Fussilat: 53]. When He mentioned the proofs of the horizons, namely the heavens and what is sent down from them of angels, and the earth and what is sent forth upon it of winds, He began with the proofs of the selves. We have already mentioned its explanation many times, and we have mentioned what has been said, that His saying ﴿from dust﴾ is a reference to the creation of Adam, and ﴿then from a drop of semen﴾ is a reference to the creation of his offspring. We have shown that the speech does not need this interpretation. Rather, ﴿He created you﴾ is addressed to people, and they are all the children of Adam, all of them from dust and from a drop of semen, because all of them come from semen, and semen comes from nourishment, and nourishment ultimately traces back to water and dust. So it is from dust that it became semen.

His saying ﴿And no female conceives or gives birth﴾ is a reference to the completeness of His knowledge (kamal al-'ilm), for what is in the wombs, before its formation (al-infikhal) and even after it, as long as it is in the belly, no one knows its condition. How, when the pregnant mother herself knows nothing of it? So when He mentioned, by His saying ﴿He created you from dust﴾, the completeness of His power, He explained, by His saying ﴿And no female conceives or gives birth except with His knowledge﴾, the completeness of His knowledge. Then He explained the pervasiveness of His will by His saying ﴿And no one is granted long life or has his life shortened except that it is in a Book﴾. Thus He made clear that He is the All-Powerful, the All-Knowing, the Willing, whereas the idols have no power, no knowledge, and no will. How, then, could any of them deserve worship?

His saying ﴿Indeed, that is easy for Allah﴾ means: the creation from dust [is easy for Him]. It is also possible that what is meant is that granting long life and shortening it are easy for Allah, and it is also possible that what is meant is that knowledge of what the female carries is easy, and all of it is easy for Allah. The first is more apt, for the usage of "easy" (yasir) is more fitting with regard to an act.

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And the two bodies of water are not alike: this one is sweet, palatable, pleasant to drink, and that one is salty, bitter. And from each you eat tender flesh and extract ornaments which you wear; and you see the ships ploughing through it, that you may seek of His bounty, and perhaps you will be grateful.﴾

Most of the exegetes said: the purpose of the verse is to draw a parable concerning disbelief and faith, or the disbeliever and the believer. Faith is not likened to disbelief in goodness and benefit, just as the two seas, the sweet and palatable and the salty and bitter, are not alike.

Upon this view, His saying ﴿And from each you eat tender flesh﴾ serves to show that the state of the disbeliever and the believer, or of disbelief and faith, is not on a par with the state of the two seas, because the bitter (sea) shares with the palatable (sea) in good and benefit, since tender flesh is found in both, ornaments are obtained from both, and ships run upon both, whereas there is no benefit in disbelief or the disbeliever. This follows the pattern of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those are like livestock; rather, they are further astray﴾ (al-A'raf: 179), and His saying: ﴿Like stones, or even harder in hardness. For indeed, among stones are those from which rivers gush forth﴾ (al-Baqarah: 74). The more apparent view is that the purpose is to mention another proof of Allah's power, in that the two seas are alike in appearance yet differ in water: one is sweet and palatable, and the other is salty and bitter. Had it been by necessity, similar things would not differ. Then, after their difference, there are things found in both that are alike: tender flesh is found in both, and ornaments are taken from both. And whoever produces difference among similar things and similarity among different things is none but a capable, choosing agent.

His saying ﴿And the two bodies of water are not alike﴾ is an indication that their non-equality is evidence of the perfection of His power and the executing of His will. In the verse there are several issues:

Issue One: The people of lexicography said: one does not say of the water of the sea, when it has saltiness, "mtill" (salty, مالح); rather it is said "milh" (brackish/saline, مِلْح). It is mentioned in some books of jurisprudence: "the water of the sea becomes salty (māli') by it," and its speaker is held to account for it; and this is more correct than what the people hold. That is because sweet water into which salt is cast until it becomes salty is only called "māli'," whereas water that is salty (milh) is said of water that has become so from its original creation, because "māli'" is a thing in which there is apparent salt to the taste, and salty water is not "water and salt"—unlike salted food. So sweet water in which salt is placed is water in which there is apparent salt to the taste, unlike that which is so by its original creation. When the jurist said, "salt is earthy, brackish particles by which the water of the sea becomes salty," he considered its origin, for he made it water neighboring salt; and the people of lexicography, when they said of the sea, "its water is milh," treated it as such from the origin of its creation. "Ujāj" means bitter.

His saying ﴿And from each you eat tender flesh﴾ refers to birds and fish; ﴿and you extract ornaments which you wear﴾ refers to pearls and coral; ﴿and you see the ships ploughing through it﴾, i.e., moving through, ploughing the sea by sailing, i.e., cutting through. His saying ﴿that you may seek of His bounty, and perhaps you will be grateful﴾ indicates what we have mentioned: that the purpose of the verse is to reason from the two seas and what is in them to the existence of Allah, His oneness, and the perfection of His power.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿He causes the night to enter into the day and causes the day to enter into the night, and He has subjected the sun and the moon, each running for a term appointed. That is God, your Lord; to Him belongs dominion. And those you invoke besides Him do not possess even a date-pit's membrane.﴾

This is another argument from the alternation of times, which we have mentioned many times. We have also mentioned that His saying after it, ﴿and He has subjected the sun and the moon﴾, is an answer to a question that the polytheists raise. They said: the alternation of night and day is due to the difference of the arcs that lie above and below the earth. In summer, the sun passes over the heads (at zenith) in some of the countries situated in the regions of the horizon, and the movement of the sun there is oblique (ḥamā'iliyyah), so it falls beneath the earth for less than half a circle during its stay beneath the earth, and therefore the night becomes short. In winter, the opposite happens, so the day becomes short. Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿and He has subjected the sun and the moon﴾, meaning: the cause of the alternation is what you have mentioned, but the course of the sun and the moon is by the will and power of God, so it is He who did that.

* * *

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿That is God, your Lord; to Him belongs dominion. And those you invoke besides Him do not possess even a date-pit's membrane.﴾

That is, He who did these things, from originating the heavens and the earth, sending the winds, sending the rains, creating man from dust, and other things, to Him belongs all dominion. There is no worshipped one except Him, by virtue of His essential perfection and because He is a King, and a king is served in proportion to his dominion. So if all dominion belongs to Him, then all worship belongs to Him. Then He clarified what contradicts the attribute of divinity, which is His saying: ﴿And those you invoke besides Him do not possess even a date-pit's membrane.﴾ Here is a subtle point: God, exalted is He, mentioned two kinds of attributes for Himself.

The first: that creation is by power and will.

The second: dominion. And He used both as evidence that He is a God who is worshipped, as He said: ﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind, the King of mankind, the God of mankind﴾ (An-Nas: 1–3). He mentioned the Lord and the King and based upon them His being God, that is, worshipped. And regarding those who associated partners with Him, He mentioned the negation of one attribute, which is the absence of dominion, by His saying: ﴿And those you invoke besides Him do not possess even a date-pit's membrane.﴾ He did not mention the negation of the other attribute, for two reasons:

The first: that all of them acknowledged that there is no creator for them except God, but they used to say that God, exalted is He, delegated the affairs of the earth and earthly things to the stars, whose idols are in their forms and ascendants. So He said: they have no dominion, and God did not grant them any dominion, nor did they possess anything.

The second: that the absence of dominion necessarily entails the absence of creation, because if he had created something he would possess it. Since they do not possess even a date-pit's membrane, they did not create anything, little or much.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿If you call upon them, they will not hear your call; and even if they heard, they would not respond to you. And on the Day of Resurrection they will disavow your association of them. And none can inform you like the One who is All-Aware.﴾

This is a refutation of what they used to say: that there is honour in worshipping idols, in terms of being close to them, looking toward them, and presenting one's needs to them, whereas God is not seen and no one can reach Him. So these people said: "They do not hear your call, but God—to Him ascends the good word, so He hears and accepts it." Then He descended from that position and said: "Grant that they hear as they suppose, for they used to say that the idols hear and know. But they could not say that they respond, because that would be a denial of what is perceived by the senses, and their not hearing is a denial of what is rationally understood. Dispute may occur over what is rationally understood, but it cannot occur over what is perceived by the senses."

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And on the Day of Resurrection they will disavow your association of them﴾. When He made clear that there is no benefit from them in this world, He made clear that there is no benefit from them in the Hereafter. Rather, He indicated that they will cause harm in the Hereafter by His saying: ﴿And on the Day of Resurrection they will disavow your association of them﴾, meaning, your associating them with God, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, association [with Him] is a great wrong﴾ [Luqman: 13], meaning, association (al-ishrak).

His saying ﴿And none can inform you like the One who is All-Aware﴾ may have two interpretations:

The first: that this is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ. Its meaning is that when God informed that the wood and the stone will speak on the Day of Resurrection and deny their worshippers, this is a matter that cannot be known by pure reason alone, were it not for God's informing about it, that they will disavow them on the Day of Resurrection. This statement, together with the fact that the report about it is a wonderful matter, is just as He said, because the One who informs about it is All-Aware.

The second: that this is an address not specific to anyone, meaning: this which has been mentioned is just as He said: ﴿And none can inform you﴾, O listener, whoever you may be, ﴿like the One who is All-Aware﴾.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿O mankind, you are the poor toward Allah, and Allah is the Free of need, the Praiseworthy.﴾

When the Prophet's (ﷺ) calling [to faith] increased and the disbelievers persisted, they said: "Perhaps Allah needs our worship, so that He commands us to it with a binding command and threatens us with a severe threat if we abandon it." So Exalted is He said: ﴿You are the poor toward Allah, and Allah is the Free of need﴾, so He does not command you to worship because of His need for you; rather, it is out of His compassion for you. There are several issues in this verse:

The first issue: Definiteness in the predicate (khabar) is rare; the more common pattern is for the predicate to be indefinite (nakirah) and the subject (mubtada') definite. This is understandable, because the speaker, in most cases, only informs about something that the one being informed does not know, or that the speaker thinks the listener has no knowledge of. Then, [the predicate] may be something known to the listener, so that the speaker says to him: "O listener, the matter you know about, you are in it, the such-and-such meaning." Like the saying of the speaker: "Zayd is standing" or "Zayd stood," meaning: Zayd, whom you know, has the attribute of standing, which you have no knowledge of. If the predicate is known to the listener, and the subject likewise, and the predicate serves as a reminder rather than a conveyance of information, then making the predicate definite is most fitting, like the saying of the speaker: "Allah is our Lord, and Muhammad is our Prophet," where the fact that Allah is Lord and that Muhammad is a Prophet is already known. Here, since the fact that people are poor is an evident matter that is hidden from no one, He said: ﴿You are the poor﴾.

The second issue: His saying "(except Allah)" is an announcement that there is no dependence except upon Him and no reliance except upon Him. This necessitates worshipping Him, since He is the one in need of whom, and the non-worship of anything other than Him, since there is no need for anything other than Him. Then He said: ﴿and Allah is the Free of need﴾, meaning: He, despite His self-sufficiency, calls you with every call, while you, because of your need, do not respond to Him or call upon Him, so that He answers you.

The third issue: Regarding His saying: ﴿the Praiseworthy﴾. When He added to the first predicate, which is His saying: ﴿You are the poor﴾, an addition, namely His saying: ﴿toward Allah﴾, as an indication of the obligation to confine worship to His worship, He added to His description as the Free of need an addition, namely that He is Praiseworthy, as an indication of your being poor, and in contrast to that, Allah is Free of need. Your need of Him, in contrast to His bounties upon you, is because He is Praiseworthy and worthy of thanks. So you are poor, while Allah is not like you in poverty; rather He is Free of need absolutely. And when you have come to need Him, He has not left you with your needs unmet; rather, He has fulfilled your needs in this world, and if you believe, He will fulfill your needs in the Hereafter, so He is the Praiseworthy.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿If He wills, He can remove you and bring a new creation﴾, as an explanation of His independence (ghina). In it there is complete eloquence (balagha), and its explanation is that He, exalted, said: ﴿If He wills, He can remove you﴾, meaning: your removal is not contingent upon anything except His will, unlike the thing one needs. For the one in need does not say about it: if so-and-so wills, he demolishes his house and destroys his property. Rather he says: were it not for the need of shelter for the house, I would have sold it, or were it not for the dependence on the property, I would have abandoned it. Then He, exalted, increased the explanation of independence with His saying: ﴿and bring a new creation﴾, meaning: if someone imagines that this king has perfection and greatness, so that if He removed him his kingship and greatness would vanish, then He is able to create a new creation better than this, more beautiful, more complete and more perfect.

* * *

Then God, exalted, said: ﴿And that is not difficult for God﴾, i.e., the removal and the bringing. Here is an issue: God has used the word ʿazīz (mighty) at times for the one who is self-subsisting, as when He said of Himself: ﴿And God was ever Strong and Mighty﴾ (al-Ahzab: 25), and said in this surah: ﴿Indeed God is Mighty, Forgiving﴾ (Fatir: 28). And He has used it for the one who depends on something else, as when He said: ﴿And that is not difficult for God﴾, and said: ﴿It is grievous to him what you suffer﴾ (al-Tawba: 128). So are these two of the same meaning or of two meanings? We say: ʿazīz in language is the one who overpowers. It is said: whoever is mighty plunders, i.e., whoever overpowers, despoils. So God is ʿazīz, i.e., overpowering. When an act is something a person cannot manage, it is said that he is overcome relative to that act. So His saying ﴿And that is not difficult for God﴾ means that act does not overpower God; rather it is easy for God. And His saying ﴿It is grievous to him what you suffer﴾ means it saddens him and harms him, like a preoccupation that overwhelms.

And His saying, exalted: ﴿No bearer bears another's burden; and if one heavily laden calls [another] to its load, nothing of it will be carried, even if he were a near relative﴾.

It is connected to what came before, because when God clarified the truth with manifest proofs and dazzling demonstrations, He mentioned what calls them to reflect upon it, saying: ﴿No bearer bears another's burden﴾, i.e., no soul bears the sin of another soul. So the Prophet (ﷺ), if he were lying in his call, would be sinful, and he believes that his sin will not be borne by you, so he guards himself and takes care. God, exalted, is not in need of your worship. So reflect and know that if you go astray, no one will bear your burden for you. It is not as your elders say: ﴿Follow our way, and we will bear your sins﴾ (al-ʿAnkabut: 12). In the verse there are issues:

The first issue: His saying ﴿wāziratun﴾ means a bearing soul. He did not say: "no soul bears the burden of another," and He did not combine the qualified and the qualifier. He did not say: "no bearing soul bears the burden (wizr) of another." For a benefit: as for the first, if He had said "no soul bears the burden of another," one would not know that every bearing soul is preoccupied with the concern of its own burden and perplexed about its affair. Another aspect: the saying "no soul bears the burden of another" may be combined with a soul that bears no burden at all, like the one protected from sin, who does not bear the burden of another and also does not bear any burden. So His saying ﴿No bearer bears﴾ clarified that it bears its own burden and does not bear the burden of others. As for omitting the mention of the qualified noun, it is because the attribute is evident and necessarily belongs to it.

Then God said: ﴿And if one heavily laden calls﴾, indicating that no one bears anything for anyone, whether unprompted or after being asked. For the one in need may be patient and his need is met without his asking; but when need reaches the limit of completeness, it compels him to ask.

The second issue: His saying ﴿heavily laden﴾ is additional clarification of what preceded. He first said ﴿No bearer bears another's burden﴾, so one might think that no one bears for another because that one is capable of carrying it, just as a strong person who holds a pomegranate or a quince in his hand is not carried for. But if the load is heavy, the carrier may be pitied and something carried for him. So He said ﴿heavily laden﴾, meaning that the absence of bearing is not because the soul is not a place of mercy through heaviness, but because the soul is heavily laden and nothing of it is carried.

The third issue: He added to that with His saying ﴿even if he were a near relative﴾, i.e., the one called, even if he were a near relative, will not bear it. In the first case it could have been said: he will not bear it because he has no connection to it, like an enemy who sees his enemy under a weight, or a stranger who sees another stranger under a load and does not carry for him. So He said ﴿even if he were a near relative﴾, meaning that all the meanings which call for carrying are present: the soul is a strong bearer capable of carrying, the other is heavily laden, and the calling soul asks, for asking is a cause of mercy if the one asked is near. Then non-carrying can only be due to an obstacle, which is that every soul is under a heavy load.

It is connected to what came before, because when God clarified the truth with manifest proofs and dazzling demonstrations, He mentioned what calls them to reflect upon it, saying: ﴿No bearer bears another's burden﴾, i.e., no soul bears the sin of another soul. God, exalted, is not in need of your worship. So reflect and know that if you go astray, no one will bear your burden for you. It is not as your elders say: ﴿Follow our way, and we will bear your sins﴾ (al-ʿAnkabut: 12). In the verse there are issues:

The first issue: His saying ﴿wāziratun﴾ means a bearing soul. He did not say: "no soul bears the burden of another," and He did not combine the qualified and the qualifier. He did not say: "no bearing soul bears the burden (wizr) of another." For a benefit: as for the first, if He had said "no soul bears the burden of another," one would not know that every bearing soul is preoccupied with the concern of its own burden and perplexed about its affair. Another aspect: the saying "no soul bears the burden of another" may be combined with a soul that bears no burden at all, like the one protected from sin, who does not bear the burden of another and also does not bear any burden. So His saying ﴿No bearer bears﴾ clarified that it bears its own burden and does not bear the burden of others. As for omitting the mention of the qualified noun, it is because the attribute is evident and necessarily belongs to it.

* * *

Then God said: ﴿And if one heavily laden calls﴾, indicating that no one bears anything for anyone, whether unprompted or after being asked. For the one in need may be patient and his need is met without his asking; but when need reaches the limit of completeness, it compels him to ask.

The second issue: His saying ﴿heavily laden﴾ is additional clarification of what preceded. He first said ﴿No bearer bears another's burden﴾, so one might think that no one bears for another because that one is capable of carrying it, just as a strong person who holds a pomegranate or a quince in his hand is not carried for. So He said ﴿heavily laden﴾, meaning that the absence of bearing is not because the soul is not a place of mercy through heaviness, but because the soul is heavily laden and nothing of it is carried.

The third issue: He added to that with His saying ﴿even if he were a near relative﴾, i.e., the one called, even if he were a near relative, will not bear it. In the first case it could have been said: he will not bear it because he has no connection to it, like an enemy who sees his enemy under a weight, or a stranger who sees another stranger under a load and does not carry for him. So He said ﴿even if he were a near relative﴾, meaning that all the meanings which call for carrying are present: the soul is a strong bearer capable of carrying, the other is heavily laden, and the calling soul asks, for asking is a cause of mercy if the one asked is near. Then non-carrying can only be due to an obstacle, which is that every soul is under a heavy load.

Then, having stated that ﴿no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾ (al-An'am: 164), He explained that good deeds benefit those who do good.

So He said: ﴿And whoever purifies himself, purifies only for his own soul﴾, meaning that his purification is for his own soul.

* * *

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And to God is the final return﴾, meaning: the one who purifies himself, if its benefit does not appear quickly, then the return to God is where it becomes manifest, on the Day of Meeting in the Abode of Permanence. And the bearer of burdens, if the consequence of his burden does not appear in this world, it appears in the Hereafter, since the return is to God.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And the blind and the seeing are not alike﴾ ﴿nor are the darknesses and the light﴾ ﴿nor the shade and the scorching heat﴾ ﴿And the living and the dead are not alike﴾.

When He had made clear guidance and misguidance, and the disbeliever did not become guided while Allah guided the believer, He set forth for them a parable of the seeing and the blind. The believer is seeing, since he perceives the clear path, and the disbeliever is blind. There are several issues (masa'il, sing. mas'alah, "question") in the interpretation of this verse.

The first issue: what is the benefit of multiplying the examples here, where He mentions the blind and the seeing, the darkness and the light, the shade and the scorching heat, and the living and the dead? We say:

The first is like the believer and the disbeliever. The believer is seeing and the disbeliever is blind. Even though the seeing person has keen sight, he sees nothing unless he is in light. So He mentioned an example for faith and unbelief and said: faith is light, the believer is seeing, and the seeing person is not hidden from light. Unbelief is darkness, and the disbeliever is blind, so he has a barrier upon a barrier. Then He mentioned an example for their final state and their return, which is the shade and the scorching heat. The believer, by his faith, is in shade and ease, and the disbeliever, by his unbelief, is in heat and hardship. Then He said: ﴿And the living and the dead are not alike﴾, as another example regarding the believer and the disbeliever, as if He said: the condition of the believer and the disbeliever is beyond the condition of the blind and the seeing, for the blind shares with the seeing a certain kind of perception, whereas the disbeliever does not perceive in a beneficial way, so he is like the dead. What we have mentioned is indicated by the fact that He repeated the verb when He first said: ﴿And the blind and the seeing are not alike﴾, and then joined the darknesses and the light and the shade and the scorching heat, and then repeated the verb, saying: ﴿And the living and the dead are not alike﴾, as if He made this to correspond to that.

The second issue: He repeated the negative particle between the darknesses and the light, the shade and the scorching heat, and the living and the dead, but did not repeat it between the blind and the seeing. This is because repetition serves emphasis, and the opposition between darkness and light, and between shade and scorching heat, is a direct contrast. Darkness opposes and contradicts light, and blindness and sight are likewise. As for the blind and the seeing, the relation is not like this, for one and the same person may be seeing and then become blind. So the blind and the seeing have no opposition between them except in terms of attribute. The opposition between shade and scorching heat is intrinsic, because what is meant by shade is the absence of heat and cold. Since the opposition there is more complete, He emphasized it by repetition. As for the living and the dead, although they are like the blind and the seeing in that one body may be a living subject of life and then become a dead subject of death, the opposition between the living and the dead is more complete than the opposition between the blind and the seeing. As we have shown, the blind and the seeing share in perceiving things, and this is not so for the living and the dead. How could it be otherwise, since the dead differ from the living in reality and not merely in attribute, as is made clear in the divine wisdom?

[Page 16]

The third issue: He placed the more noble in two examples, namely the shade and the scorching heat, and placed it later in two examples, namely sight and light. Regarding such cases the commentators say that it is for the harmony of the final rhyme of the verses (tawakhi awakhir al-ayy). This is weak, because the harmony of final sounds goes back to saj' (rhymed prose), whereas the miraculous quality of the Qur'an lies in its meaning and not merely in its wording. The poet advances and postpones for the sake of rhyme, so the wording compels him to change the meaning. But the Qur'an is perfect wisdom; its meaning is sound and its wording eloquent, so it does not advance or postpone a word without meaning. We say: before the Prophet ﷺ the disbelievers were in misguidance, so they were like the blind, and their path was like darkness. Then when the Prophet ﷺ came and made the truth clear, and some of them were guided by it and became seeing, their path became like light. So He said: the one who was upon disbelief before the mission is not alike to the one who was guided after it to faith. Since disbelief preceded faith in the time of Muhammad ﷺ, and the disbeliever came before the believer, He placed the earlier first. Then when He mentioned the final state and the return, He placed what relates to mercy before what relates to wrath, in keeping with His saying in the matters of divine attributes: "My mercy precedes My wrath." Then the persistent disbeliever after the mission became more misguided than the blind and resembled the dead in lacking perception of the truth in every respect. So He said: ﴿And the living and the dead are not alike﴾, that is, the believers who believed in what Allah sent down, and the dead, who had the clear verses recited to them and did not benefit from them. These latter came after the faith of those who believed, so He placed them after the believers because the life of the believers existed before the death of the stubborn disbelievers. And He placed the blind before the seeing because the misguided disbelievers existed before the mission before the guided believers who came after it.

The fourth issue: If you say: He matched the blind with the seeing in the singular, and likewise the shade with the scorching heat, and He matched the living with the dead in the plural, and He matched the darknesses with the light, using the plural in one and the singular in the other, do you know any wisdom in this? I say: yes, by Allah's favour and guidance. As for the blind and the seeing and the shade and the scorching heat, it is because He matched the genus with the genus and did not mention individuals. For among the blind and those who possess sight there may be an individual of one kind who equals an individual of the other kind, such as a seeing stranger in a place, or a blind native of that place. A blind man may be able to reach a destination when a seeing man cannot, or a blind man may have such intelligence that he equals a dull seeing man. So the difference between the two kinds is certain, for the kind of the seeing is better than the kind of the blind. As for the living and the dead, the difference between them is greater, for no dead person equals a living person in perception. So He stated that the living are not equal to the dead, whether you match genus with genus or individual with individual. As for the darknesses and the light, the truth is one, namely monotheism, while falsehood is many, namely the paths of association, as we have shown, for some of them worship the stars, some worship fire, and some worship idols shaped like angels, and other things besides. The difference between each one of those individual falsehoods and this single truth is clear. So He said: all the darknesses, when you consider them, you will not find among them anything equal to the light. We have already mentioned, in the commentary on His saying: ﴿And He made the darknesses and the light﴾ (al-An'am: 1), the reason for the singular of light and the plural of darkness. Among its causes: light does not exist except with the presence of a source of light, a receptive place capable of being illuminated, and the absence of any barrier between the light and what is illuminated. For example, when the sun rises and there is a place receptive to illumination, which is that which holds the ray, then a room that has an opening through which the ray enters, and opposite the opening there is an exit through which the ray leaves and enters another room and spreads the ray over its floor, the second room is seen as lit and the first as dark. But if there is no barrier, as in a room that has no opening, it does not become lit. So when the three conditions are met, the room is illuminated; otherwise darkness is not realized, since the absence of any one of the three conditions prevents it.

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And there is no nation but that a warner has passed among them﴾, establishing two matters:
One of them: to console his heart, since he knows that others before him were like him, bearing the harm of their people.

The second: to oblige the people to accept him, for he is not an innovation among the messengers; rather he is like others who claim what the messengers claimed and affirm it.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if they deny you, those before them have indeed denied; their messengers came to them with clear proofs, and with the scriptures and the illuminating Book.﴾

That is: you came to them with the clear proof and the Book, so they denied you and harmed you; and others also came to them with the like of that, and they did to them what they did to you, and they endured what they were denied. Thus We oblige them that whoever came before from the messengers was not known to be messengers except by clear miracles; and We have given those to Muhammad ﷺ — ﴿and with the scriptures and the illuminating Book﴾ — and all of them We have given to Muhammad. So he is a messenger like the messengers, and their acceptance of him is binding, just as the acceptance of Moses and Jesus, peace be upon them all, is binding. This is an affirmation addressed to the People of the Book. Know that He, exalted is He, mentioned three things:

The first of them: the clear proofs (al-bayyinat). This is because every messenger must have a miracle, which is the lowest of the ranks. Then a book may be sent down to him containing admonitions and reminders, even if it has no abrogation and no legislated rulings that abrogate a law. Whoever receives something like this is higher in rank than one who does not receive it. Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 35, verses 26–27:

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Then I seized those who disbelieved, so how was My rejection?﴾

That is: whoever denied the Book sent down before and the Messenger, Allah the Exalted seized him. Likewise, whoever denies the Prophet, peace be upon him, [will be seized]. His saying ﴿so how was My rejection?﴾ is a question for affirmation, for they knew the severity of Allah's rejection of them and the terrible matter that came upon them of total annihilation.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Have you not seen that Allah sends down water from the sky, and We bring forth thereby fruits of varying colours?﴾

This is an argument (istidlal, inference from evidence) by another proof for the oneness of Allah and His power. In its interpretation there are issues (masa'il, points of discussion):

Issue one: He mentioned this proof in the form of a question, saying ﴿Have you not seen﴾, while He mentioned the previous proof in the form of a statement, saying ﴿And it is Allah who sends the winds﴾. There are two aspects to this:

The first: the sending down of water is closer to benefit, and its benefit is more evident, for it is not hidden from anyone who looks that water is the source of the earth's life. So He magnified its indication by means of the interrogative, because the interrogative used for affirmation is only said of something very manifest. This is like someone who sees the crescent moon, which is very faint, and another asks him, "Where is it?" He says, "In such-and-such a place." If the other does not see it, he says to him, "You are right, it is faint, and you are excused." And if it is clearly visible, he says to him, "Do you not see it? This is plainly visible."

The second: He mentioned it after establishing the matter by another proof, and the one addressed had, by what came before, become perceptive of the ways of indication. So He said to him: "You have become perceptive of what We have mentioned, and no excuse remains for you. Do you not see this verse?"

Issue two: Who is the one addressed? It may be one of two:

One of them: the Prophet (ﷺ). In this there is wisdom: when Allah, exalted is He, had mentioned the proofs and they did not benefit those people, He broke off speech with them and turned to others. This is like a master who advises some of his slaves and prevents them from corruption, but guidance does not benefit them. He says to another: "Listen, and do not be like these," and he repeats with him what he had said to the first. This implies that the first has a deficiency and is not worthy of being addressed, so he takes heed of it and removes that deficiency from himself.

The other: that the speech does not go out to something foreign to the first, but rather comes with what is close to it, lest the first hear a different speech and leave off reflecting on what he was in, namely the admonition.

Issue three: This is an argument for the power and free choice of Allah, in that from one water He brought forth fruits of different kinds. In it there are subtleties:

The first: He said "sent down" and He said "We brought forth."

We have already mentioned its benefit, and we repeat it: Allah, exalted is He, said ﴿Have you not seen that Allah sent down﴾. If the ignorant person says, "The descent of water is by nature, because of its weight," it is said to him: "As for bringing forth, you cannot say of it that it is by nature. Rather it is by the will of Allah." When this was made clear, He attributed it to the speaker.

Another aspect: when Allah, exalted is He, said ﴿that Allah sent down﴾, He made Himself known by an indication, and the one reflecting on it drew near to Allah, exalted is He, and became one of those present, so He said to him "We brought forth," because of His nearness.

A third aspect: bringing forth is a more complete blessing than sending down, because sending down is for the sake of bringing forth. So He attributed the more complete to Himself in the first person form of the speaker, and what is less than it in the third person form of the absent.

The first: that it is for *istinaf* (resumption of speech). The second: that it is for *'atf* (conjunction). Its implied sense is: "and He created, from the mountains..."

Then He added explanation and said "of varying hues." Likewise, the mountains themselves are a proof of power and choice, because the fact that mountains are in some regions of the earth and not in others, and the variation in the form of a mountain, for some are lower and some higher, is a proof of power and choice.
