**The second subtle point:** God, the Exalted, says: ﴿And among the mountains are streaks, white and red, of varying hues, and deep black﴾ ﴿And among people and beasts and cattle are those of varying hues likewise﴾.

It may be said: "The variation in fruits is due to the variation in lands. Do you not see that some plants do not grow in some lands, such as saffron and others?" God, the Exalted, answers: the variation of lands is only by the will of God. Otherwise, why would some mountains have red places and white places? *Judad* (streaks) is the plural of *juddah*, which means a stretch of land or a path.

If it is asked: what is the function of the *waw* (and) in ﴿And among the mountains﴾? We say it may bear two meanings:

The first: that it is for *istinaf* (resumption of speech). It is as if He said: "And We brought forth with water fruits of varying colors, and among the existing things are, from the mountains, white streaks, which indicate power and refute those who deny the will in the variation of the colors of fruits."

The second: that it is for *'atf* (conjunction). Its implied sense is: "and He created, from the mountains..."

Al-Zamakhshari said: "He meant: [there are] those with streaks."

**The third subtle point:** He mentioned the mountains and did not mention the earth, as He said elsewhere: ﴿And in the earth are neighboring tracts﴾ (al-Ra'd: 4), although this proof is similar to that. This is because God, when He mentioned in the first verse ﴿So We brought forth thereby fruits﴾, the very bringing forth of fruits was a proof of power. Then He added explanation and said "of varying hues." Likewise, the mountains themselves are a proof of power and choice, because the fact that mountains are in some regions of the earth and not in others, and the variation in the form of a mountain, for some are lower and some higher, is a proof of power and choice. Then He added further explanation and said: "streaks, white," meaning that along with their being a proof in themselves, they are also a proof through the variation of their colors, just as the bringing forth of fruits is in itself a proof, and the variation of their colors is also a proof.

**The fourth issue:** "of varying hues" (*mukhtalif alwanuha*). The apparent meaning is that the variation returns to each color: white ones of varying hues and red ones of varying hues. This is because white may be the color of *jiss* (gypsum/plaster) or the color of white earth less white than gypsum, and likewise red. If the intended meaning were that the white and the red are of varying hues, it would be mere emphasis, and the first is preferable. On this basis, we say: He did not mention "of varying hues" after the white, red and black together. Rather, He mentioned it after the white and red and placed the deep black afterwards, because when He mentioned black together with the intensifier, namely *gharabib* (intensely black), it reaches the utmost degree of blackness, so there is no variation in it.

**The fifth issue:** It has been said that *gharibib* is an intensifier of *aswad* (black); one says "aswad gharibib" (intensely black). An intensifier comes only after what it intensifies, so how did ﴿gharabib sud﴾ come? We say: al-Zamakhshari said: "*Gharabib* is an intensifier for a color that is implied in the speech, as if He, the Exalted, said: 'the blackness of *gharabib*,' and then He repeated *sud* (black) a second time, and in this there is a benefit, which is the increase of emphasis, because He mentioned it both implicitly and explicitly." Some said: it is by inversion (*taqdim* and *ta'khir*).

Then God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And among people and beasts and cattle﴾, as a further proof of His power and will. It is as if God divided the signs of creation in the world in which we are, which is the world of compounds, into two parts: animal and non-animal. Non-animal is either a plant or a mineral. The plant is nobler. He indicated it by His words ﴿So We brought forth thereby fruits﴾. Then He mentioned the mineral by His words ﴿And among the mountains﴾. Then He mentioned the animal and began with the nobler of them, which is the human, so He said ﴿And among people﴾. Then He mentioned the beasts, because their benefit is in their life, and the cattle, whose benefit is in eating from them. Or, because *dabbah* (beast) in common usage is applied to the horse, which after the human is nobler than others. His saying ﴿of varying hues likewise﴾ is in the masculine form because the human is among those mentioned, and the masculine is higher and more appropriate.

* *

Then God the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, those who fear God among His servants are the scholars. Indeed, God is Exalted in Might, Forgiving﴾.

Fear (*khashyah*) is in proportion to the knowledge of the one feared, and the scholar knows God, so he fears Him and hopes in Him. This is evidence that the scholar is higher in rank than the worshipper, because God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of God is the most righteous of you﴾ (al-Hujurat: 13). So He made clear that honor is in proportion to piety, and piety is in proportion to knowledge.

Thus honor is in proportion to knowledge, not to action. Yes, if the scholar abandons action, that impairs his knowledge, for whoever sees him will say: "If he had known, he would have acted." Then God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, God is Exalted in Might, Forgiving﴾, mentioning what requires fear and hope. His being *'azīz* (mighty), possessing retribution, requires complete fear, and His being *ghafur* (forgiving) of what is less than that requires far-reaching hope. The reading of the one who read *al-'ulama'* with a *fatha* (accusative) and *Allah* with a *damma* (nominative) means: "Only those who glorify and revere Him [fear Him]."

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, those who recite the Book of Allah﴾.

When He mentioned the scholars of Allah, their fear of Him, and their honour because of their fear, He mentioned the scholars of the Book of Allah who act upon what is in it. His saying ﴿those who recite the Book of Allah﴾ is an indication of remembrance (dhikr).

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and establish the prayer﴾ is an indication of bodily action.

His saying ﴿and spend out of what We have provided them﴾ is an indication of action with wealth. In these two verses there is profound wisdom. His saying "only those among His servants who have knowledge fear Allah" is an indication of the action of the heart; His saying ﴿Indeed, those who recite﴾ is an indication of the action of the tongue; and His saying ﴿and establish the prayer and spend out of what We have provided them﴾ is an indication of the action of the limbs. Then these three things are connected to the side of magnifying Allah and compassion towards His creation, because we have explained that whoever magnifies a king, when he sees one of the king's servants in need, it is incumbent upon him to meet that need, and if he neglects it, he undermines the magnification. To this He alluded with His saying (in the hadith): "My servant, I fell ill and you did not visit Me." The servant will say, "How could You fall ill, when You are the Lord of the worlds?" Allah will say, "My servant so-and-so fell ill and you did not visit him; had you visited him, you would have found Me with him." That is: magnification is connected with compassion, so where there is no compassion for the creatures of Allah, there is no magnification of the side of Allah.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿secretly and openly﴾ is an exhortation to spend in whatever way is possible: if it is possible secretly, that is well and good; otherwise, openly. Let not the suspicion that it might be showing off prevent him, for abandoning good out of fear that it will be said of him that he is a show-off is itself pure showing off. It is possible that what is meant by His saying ﴿secretly﴾ is voluntary charity (sadaqah), and ﴿openly﴾ is obligatory zakat, since openly giving zakat is like openly fulfilling an obligation, and it is recommended.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿they hope for a commerce that will never perish﴾ is an indication of sincerity (ikhlas), meaning: they spend not so that it may be said that he is generous, nor for any of the things other than the Face of Allah, for whatever is other than Allah is perishing, and the merchant in it has a perished trade.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿that He may pay them their rewards﴾ means what they expect, even if it be something of the utmost magnitude; ﴿and increase them of His bounty﴾ means He gives them what did not occur to their minds at the time of action. It is also possible that the increase is the gaze upon Him, as has been reported in the explanation of the increase. ﴿Indeed, He is Forgiving﴾ in giving the rewards; ﴿Appreciative﴾ in giving the increase.

* * *
Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And what We have revealed to you of the Book is the truth﴾.

When He had explained the first foundation, which is the existence of the One God, by various kinds of proofs from His saying ﴿And Allah is He who sends the winds﴾, His saying ﴿And Allah created you﴾, and His saying ﴿Do you not see that Allah sends down﴾, He mentioned the second foundation, which is prophethood, saying ﴿And what We have revealed to you of the Book is the truth﴾. Also, it is as if He had mentioned that those who recite the Book of Allah, Allah will give them their full reward, and so He said ﴿And what We have revealed to you of the Book is the truth﴾, confirming the reward and recompense He had explained for reciting the Book of Allah, for it is truth and sincerity; so its reciter is one who is right and one who makes right. Concerning its explanation there are several issues:

The first issue: His saying ﴿of the Book﴾ may be for the beginning of the extent (ibtida' al-ghayah), as one says: "A letter was sent to me from the Amir or the governor." On this basis, the Book may mean the Preserved Tablet, meaning: what We have revealed to you from the Preserved Tablet is true. It may also mean the Qur'an, meaning the guidance and clarification which We have revealed to you from the Qur'an. It may be for explanation (bayan), as one says: "A consignment of clothing and cloth was sent to so-and-so."

The second issue: His saying ﴿it is the truth﴾ is more emphatic than the speaker's saying "what We have revealed to you is true," in two respects:

The first: the definite form of the predicate indicates that the matter is in the utmost clarity, because a predicate is usually indefinite, since informing in most cases is conveying the establishment of a matter which the hearer does not know, regarding something the hearer knows, as in our saying "Zayd stood." The hearer should know Zayd, and not know that he stood, so one informs him of it. If the predicate is also known, then the informing is for alerting, and both are defined with the article, as in our saying "Zayd is the scholar in this city" when his knowledge is well known.

* *
The third issue: His saying ﴿confirming what is before it﴾ is a circumstantial clause emphasising that it is truth, for when the truth is such that there is no contradiction between it and the books of Allah, it is free from the possibility of falsehood. In His saying "confirming" there is an affirmation that it is revelation, because when the Prophet ﷺ was neither a reader nor a writer, and yet brought an explanation of what is in the books of Allah, this could only be from Allah, exalted is He. It was also an answer to the question of the disbelievers, for they used to say that the Torah contains such-and-such, and the Gospel mentions such-and-such, and they used to invent [doctrines] such as the Trinity and others, and they used to say that the Qur'an contains something different from that. He said: as for the Torah and the Gospel, no trust remains in them because of your alteration; but this Qur'an, whatever is in it which is in the Torah is true and remains as it was revealed, and whatever is not in it, or is contrary to it, is not from the Torah. So the Qur'an confirms the Torah.

There is another aspect: that this revelation confirms what came before it, for if revelation did not exist, Moses and Jesus, peace be upon them both, would have lied about the sending down of the Torah and the Gospel. When revelation is found and descends upon Muhammad ﷺ, its permissibility is known and what came before is confirmed by it. On this basis there is a subtle point: Allah made the Qur'an a confirmer of what passed, although what passed is also a confirmer of it, because when revelation descends upon one person, it is permissible for it to descend upon another, namely Muhammad ﷺ. He did not make what came before a confirmer of the Qur'an, because the Qur'an's being a miracle suffices for its confirmation as revelation, whereas for what came before, a miracle must accompany it to confirm it.

**Issue 4:** His saying, ﴿Indeed, Allah is Acquainted with His servants, Seeing﴾, has two interpretations.

The first: it confirms that this (the Qur'an) is the truth, because it is a revelation from Allah, and Allah is Acquainted (*khabir*), knowing what is hidden, and Seeing (*basir*), knowing what is apparent. So it cannot be false in its revelation, neither in what is hidden nor in what is apparent.

The second: it is a response to what they used to say, that it was not sent down to a great man. It is said: Indeed Allah is Acquainted with His servants, knowing their inner states, and Seeing, observing their outward conduct. So He chose Muhammad (ﷺ) and did not choose anyone else, and he is the most suitable of all.

* * *

Then He, exalted, said: ﴿Then We caused to inherit the Book those whom We chose of Our servants. Among them is one who wrongs himself, among them is one who is moderate, and among them is one who outstrips others in good deeds by the permission of Allah.﴾ Most of the exegetes agree that "the Book" means the Qur'an. On this view, those whom We chose are those who took hold of the Book, and they are the believers, and the one who wrongs himself, the moderate one and the foremost one are all among them. This is supported by His saying, ﴿Gardens of perpetual residence, which they will enter﴾ (al-Ra'd 13:23), which informs that they enter Paradise. The phrase ﴿then We caused to inherit﴾ also indicates this, because inheritance comes after the revelation, and there is no Book after the Qur'an. It is the inherited thing, and the inheritance here means giving after the departure of the one who held the thing given. It may also be said that "the Book" refers to the category of Books, as in His saying, ﴿Their messengers came to them with clear proofs, with scriptures, and with the illuminating Book﴾ (Fatir 35:25). The meaning on this view is: We gave the Book to those whom We chose, and they are the Prophets. This is supported by the fact that the term "chosen" (*al-mustafa*) is applied to the Prophets frequently, and not so to others. Also, His saying, ﴿of Our servants﴾, indicates that the servants are honored and dignified through their attribution to Him. Furthermore, those chosen from among them are more noble than them, and it is not fitting for one who is more noble than the noble to be a wrongdoer, especially since Allah applies the term "wrongdoer" (*zalim*) in many places to the disbeliever, and calls shirk (association of partners with Allah) "injustice."

According to the first, apparent view, its meaning is explained as follows: We gave the Qur'an to those who believed in Muhammad and took it from him, and they then differed. ﴿Among them is one who wrongs himself﴾, who is the evildoer; ﴿among them is one who is moderate﴾, who mixed a righteous deed with a wicked one; ﴿among them is one who outstrips others in good deeds﴾, who sincerely performed the deed for Allah and purified it from misdeeds. If someone asks: how does He say of those whom He described as His servants and as chosen, that among them is one who is a wrongdoer, when the term "wrongdoer" is applied to the disbeliever in many places? We reply: the believer, when committing disobedience, places himself in other than its proper place, so he is a wrongdoer to himself during the act of disobedience. The Prophet (ﷺ) pointed to this when he said: "The fornicator does not commit fornication while he is a believer." This is confirmed by the statement of Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, who narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Our wrongdoer is forgiven." Adam (peace be upon him), despite being chosen, said: ﴿Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves﴾ (al-A'raf 7:23). As for the disbeliever, he places his heart, by which the body is guided, in other than its proper place, so he is a wrongdoer absolutely. As for the heart of the believer, it is at rest in faith, and he places in it nothing but reflection on the blessings of Allah, and he places in it nothing but love for Allah.

There are many opinions concerning the three ranks:

First: the wrongdoer is the one whose bad deeds outweigh his good deeds; the moderate one is the one whose bad and good deeds are equal; and the foremost is the one whose good deeds outweigh.

Second: the wrongdoer is the one whose outward appearance is better than his inward state; the moderate one is the one whose outward and inward states are equal; and the foremost is the one whose inward state is better.

Third: the wrongdoer is the monotheist whose tongue professes monotheism but whose limbs contradict it; the moderate one is the monotheist who restrains his limbs from contradicting it through obligation; and the foremost is the monotheist whom monotheism makes forget everything but monotheism itself.

Fourth: the wrongdoer is the one who commits a major sin; the moderate one is the one who commits a minor sin; and the foremost is the one who is protected from sin.

Fifth: the wrongdoer is the reciter of the Qur'an who does not know it and does not act upon its ruling; the moderate one is the reciter who knows it; and the foremost is the reciter who knows it and acts upon it.

Sixth: the wrongdoer is the ignorant; the moderate one is the student; and the foremost is the scholar.

Seventh: the wrongdoers are the companions of the left (*ashab al-mash'ama*); the moderate ones are the companions of the right (*ashab al-maymana*); and the foremost are the foremost, those brought near (al-Waqi'a 56:10–11).

Eighth: the wrongdoer is the one who is brought to account and enters the Fire; the moderate one is the one who is brought to account and enters Paradise; and the foremost is the one who enters Paradise without reckoning.

Ninth: the wrongdoer is the one persisting in disobedience; the moderate one is the one who regrets and repents; and the foremost is the one whose repentance is accepted.

Tenth: the wrongdoer is the one who took the Qur'an but did not act upon it; the moderate one is the one who acted upon it; and the foremost is the one who took it, acted upon it, and explained to the people how to act upon it, so they acted upon it by his word. Thus he is both perfect and one who perfects others. The moderate one is perfect, and the wrongdoer is deficient. The preferred view is that the wrongdoer is the one who departed from obedience, abandoned the commands of Allah, and committed what He forbade, for he has placed a thing in other than its proper place. The moderate one is the one who strives to avoid transgression, and even if he is not granted success in that, and a sin escapes him and a wrong proceeds from him, he is still moderate, striving, and intending the truth. The foremost one is the one who does not transgress, by the grace of Allah. This is indicated by His saying, ﴿by the permission of Allah﴾, meaning: he strove and was granted success in what he strove for. And in what he strove for, he is foremost in good: good occurs in his heart and he hastens to it before the self can beautify something else. The moderate one has good occur in his heart, but the self makes him hesitate. The wrongdoer is overcome by the self. To put it another way: whoever is overcome by the commanding self and obeys it is a wrongdoer; whoever struggles against his self, sometimes prevailing and sometimes being overcome, is the moderate one; and whoever subdues his self is the foremost.

As for His saying, ﴿That is the great bounty﴾, it may have several meanings:

First: the success indicated by His saying, ﴿by the permission of Allah, that is the great bounty﴾.

Second: outstripping others in good deeds is the great bounty.

Third: the inheritance is a great bounty. This is according to the well-known interpretation. As for the other view, namely that ﴿Then We caused to inherit the Book﴾ means the category of the Book, as He said, ﴿Their messengers came to them with clear proofs, with scriptures, and with the illuminating Book﴾ (Fatir 35:25), questions arise against it:

First: "thumma" (then) indicates a delay, and the giving of the Book did not occur after the revelation to Muhammad (ﷺ). So what is meant by the word "thumma"? We reply: its meaning is that Allah is Acquainted and Seeing; He informed them and saw them, then He caused them to inherit the Book. It is as if He said: We knew the inner states and saw the outward appearances, so We chose servants, ﴿then We caused to inherit the Book﴾.

Second: how can there be a wrongdoer to himself among the Prophets? We reply: "among them" does not refer to the chosen Prophets. Rather the meaning is: what We revealed to you is the truth, and you are the chosen one, just as We chose messengers and gave them scriptures. "Among them," that is, among your people, is one who wrongs himself, who disbelieved in you and in what was sent down to you; and one who is moderate, who believed in you but did not carry out all that I commanded him; and one who is foremost, who believed and did righteous deeds.

Third: His saying, ﴿Gardens of perpetual residence, which they will enter﴾. Those who enter are those mentioned. According to what you have said, the wrongdoer would not enter. We reply: those who enter are the foremost. As for the moderate one, his matter is suspended, or he enters the Fire and then enters Paradise. The explanation applies to the first matter and not to what follows it. This is indicated by His saying, ﴿They will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold﴾ and His saying, ﴿Praise be to Allah, who has removed from us grief﴾ (Fatir 35:34).

Then He said: ﴿Gardens of Eden which they will enter. Therein they will be adorned with bracelets of gold and pearls, and their clothing therein will be silk.﴾

As to those who enter, there are several views:

First: they are the three categories, according to our view that the wrongdoer, the moderate and the foremost are categories of the believers.

Second: they are those who recite the Book of Allah.

Third: they are the foremost (al-sabiqun), and this is the strongest view, because of the proximity of their mention, and because He mentioned their honouring with His words ﴿they will be adorned﴾; so the one honoured is the foremost. On this view there are several discussions:

The first: placing the agent before the verb and delaying the object after it accords with the order of meaning when the object is a real one, as in our saying: ﴿Allah created the heavens﴾ (Ibrahim: 19) and the speaker's saying: Zayd built the wall. For Allah exists before everything; then He has an act, which is creation; then the object, which is the heavens, results from it. Likewise Zayd exists before the building, and then the wall is from his building. But when the object is not a real one, as in our saying: Zayd entered the house and struck 'Amr, the house is in reality not an object of the one who enters; rather it is one of his actions which is realized in relation to the house. Likewise 'Amr is one of the actions of Zayd which was connected to him, and so he is called an object. This order does not arise. Yet the original principle is placing the agent before the object, and for this reason the fronted object is repeated by a pronoun. You say: ʿAmran darabahu Zayd (As for ʿAmr, Zayd struck him), so you place it after the verb with the pronoun ha' referring back to it. In that case the speech becomes lengthy, and the wise speaker does not choose it except for a benefit. So what is the benefit in fronting the gardens before the verb which is "entering", and repeating their mention by the pronoun in "yadkhuluna-ha" (they enter them), and what is the difference between this and the speaker's saying "yadkhuluna jannati ʿadn" (they enter gardens of Eden)? We say: the hearer, when he knows that he has an entrance among the entrances and that he has an entering but does not know the specific entrance, remains with his heart attached, wondering which entrance it will be. When it is said to him, "You enter," then until he hears "the house" or "the market" he remains attached in heart as to which of the entrances it is. But when it is said to him, "You enter the house of Zayd," then by mentioning the house he knows his entrance, and by what he already has of prior knowledge that he has an entering, he knows the entering, so no hesitation remains for him. This is especially so with Paradise and Hell, for between the two entrances there is a vast distance.

The second: His saying ﴿Therein they will be adorned﴾ indicates the speed of entry, for if the adornment took place outside, there would be a delay in entering. Thus He said ﴿they will enter them﴾ and in them their adornment takes place.

The third: His saying ﴿of bracelets﴾ uses the plural of plural, for it is the plural of ʾasāwir, which is itself the plural of siwār. His saying ﴿and their clothing therein will be silk﴾ is not like this, because excess in clothing indicates a need to ward off cold or something else, whereas excess in adornment indicates nothing but wealth.

The fourth: He mentioned bracelets among the rest of the ornaments in many places, including His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and they will be adorned with bracelets of silver﴾ (al-Insan: 21). This is because adornment has two meanings:

One of them: showing that the one adorned is not degraded by occupations, for adornment does not occur during cooking or washing.

The second of them: showing independence from things and showing power over things. This is because adornment is either with pearls and jewels, or with gold and silver. Adorning oneself with jewels and pearls indicates that the one adorned is not unable to reach great things when needed, whereas he is unable to reach things that are scarce in existence without need. Adorning oneself with gold and silver indicates that he is not in essential need, for otherwise he would spend the gold and silver on meeting the need. Once you know this, we say: bracelets have their place on the hands, and most works are done by the hand, since it is for grasping. So when they are adorned with bracelets, it is known that they are free from work. Gold and pearls are an indication of the two kinds from which ornament is made.

Then God Most High said: ﴿And they will say, "All praise is due to God, who has removed from us the grief. Indeed, our Lord is Forgiving and Appreciative."﴾

Regarding "grief" (al-hazan), there are many opinions, but the most appropriate is to say: the intended meaning is the removal of every grief. The definite article (alif and lam) is for the genus and its comprehensiveness. The removal of grief comes through the attainment of everything that is fitting and its enduring forever, for if any part of it were not attained, grief would exist because of its absence; and if it were attained but did not endure, grief would not be fully gone, because of its cessation and the fear of losing it. As for His words, ﴿Indeed, our Lord is Forgiving and Appreciative﴾, God has mentioned about them matters that all indicate honor from God.

The first: praise (al-hamd), for the one who praises is rewarded.

The second: their saying "our Lord" (rabbana), for God is never called upon with this word except that He responds to them, unless the one calling has wasted the required time or asked for what is not permissible, such as being returned to the world from the Hereafter.

The third: their saying ﴿Forgiving﴾.

The fourth: their saying ﴿Appreciative﴾. The "Forgiving" points to His forgiving them in the Hereafter in return for the praise they offered in this world, and the "Appreciative" points to His giving them and increasing for them because of the praise He found from them in the Hereafter.

* * *

Then God Most High said: ﴿Who has settled us in the abode of permanence by His bounty﴾, meaning the abode of residence (al-iqamah). When God mentioned their joy and honor through being adorned and admitted into the Gardens, He explained their joy in remaining therein and informed them of its permanence, as they said: ﴿Who has settled us in the abode of permanence﴾, meaning the residence. The maf'ul (object form) often comes in the sense of the masdar (verbal noun) from every form, as one says, "ma lahu ma'quul," meaning "ʿaql" (reason). God Most High said: ﴿an entrance of truthfulness﴾ (al-Isra' 80), and He said: ﴿And We tore them completely apart﴾ (Saba' 19), and likewise mustakhraj for istikhraj (extraction). This is because the masdar is in reality the maf'ul, for it is what was done, so it is permissible to place the maf'ul in its position. In His words ﴿the abode of permanence﴾ there is an indication that this world is a station where the responsible person alights, and from which he departs to the station of the graves, and from there to the station of the plain where there is gathering and from it separation. For some, the Fire may be another station, while the Garden is the abode of permanence, and likewise the Fire is for its people. Their words ﴿by His bounty﴾ mean by the ruling of His promise, not by an obligation upon Him from anyone else.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 35, verses 35–36:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿No weariness touches us therein, nor does fatigue touch us therein﴾. Al-lughub (fatigue) is exhaustion (al-i'a'), and al-nasab (weariness) is the cause of exhaustion. If someone says: when He has stated that ﴿no weariness touches them therein﴾, it is known that ﴿no weariness touches us therein﴾, and a wise speaker does not negate the cause and then negate its effect by a conjunction. So one does not say: "I did not eat and I was not satisfied," or "I did not stand and I did not walk," and the reverse is common. Rather, one says: "I was not satisfied, nor did I eat," because the negation of satiety does not necessarily entail the negation of eating. The context of what has been established is that one should say: "No exhaustion touches us therein and no hardship." Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 35, verses 37–38:

﴿And they will cry out therein.﴾ That is, it will not be lightened. Even if they cry out and writhe, God will not lighten it for them out of His bounty until they ask Him; rather they will ask and will not find [relief]. In this there is an indication that their being pained is punishment and not discipline, for the one being disciplined, when he says to his disciplinarian, "I will not return to what I did," and "how evil what I did was," he is left alone; but the one being punished is not.

This is because the imprisoned person is patient, perhaps he will come out without asking; but when his stay lengthens, he seeks release without binding himself by an oath; if he is not ransomed, he binds himself with an oath and says, "Release me, and I will do such and such."

On this basis they said: ﴿we will do righteousness﴾, resolutely, without seeking God's help and without any reservation about it, and they did not say: "The matter is in God's hand." It is as if God the Exalted, just as He did not guide them in the world, did not guide them in the Hereafter. Then Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿It is He who has made you successors upon the earth﴾.

This confirms the cutting-off of their argument. When they said, ﴿Our Lord, bring us back so we may do righteousness﴾, and Allah, the Exalted, said, ﴿Did We not give you life long enough for whoever would take heed to take heed?﴾, this indicates that the granting of power and the respite, a period in which knowledge is possible, has already occurred, and you did not believe. He added to this with His words, ﴿and there had come to you the warner﴾, meaning: We gave you intellects, and We sent to you one who supports the rational (al-ma'qul, the intellect-based, 'aqli) with the transmitted proof (al-manqul, the revealed, naqli). He added to that with His words, Exalted is He, ﴿It is He who has made you successors upon the earth﴾, meaning: He warned you through those who passed before and the condition of those who came to an end. For if knowledge had not come to you that whoever denied the messengers was destroyed, your obstinacy would have been more hidden and your corruption lighter. But you were given respite, given life, and commanded through the messengers with what you were commanded, and made successors upon the earth, meaning successor after successor, so that you know the state of those who passed away and, having seen their state, you become content with it. ﴿Whoever disbelieves﴾ after all this, ﴿upon him is his disbelief, and the disbelief of the disbelievers does not increase them in the sight of their Lord except in hatred﴾, because the earlier disbeliever was already hated, like a servant who does not serve his master. The later one, whom the messenger warned and who did not take heed, is more hated, like a servant whom an advisor counsels, commanding him to serve his master, promising him and threatening him, yet the counsel does not benefit him nor make him happy. And the one who comes after them, who saw the punishment of those who preceded and did not fear its punishment, is the most hated of all.

* * *

Then Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And the disbelief of the disbelievers does not increase them except in loss﴾. That is: disbelief is of no benefit in the sight of Allah, since it increases only hatred; nor does it benefit them in themselves, since it gives them nothing but loss. For life is like capital: whoever spends it seeking the pleasure of Allah profits, and whoever spends it seeking His wrath incurs loss.

* * *

Then Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Say, "Have you considered your partners whom you invoke besides Allah? Show me what they have created from the earth, or do they have a partnership in the heavens? Or have We given them a book so that they are upon clear evidence from it? Rather, the wrongdoers promise one another nothing but delusion."﴾

This confirms monotheism (tawhid, the oneness of God) and refutes association (shirk, associating partners with God). His words, ﴿Have you considered﴾, mean: inform me, because the interrogative requires an answer. One says, "Have you considered what Zayd did?" and the listener says, "He sold or he bought." Were it not that it implies the meaning of "inform me," the answer would only be "No" or "Yes." His words, ﴿your partners﴾: He attributed the partners to them only because the idols in reality were not partners of Allah; rather, they made them partners. So He said "your partners," meaning the partners by your making. It may also be said: "your partners" means your partners in the Fire, based on His words, ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah are the fuel of Hell﴾ (al-Anbiya': 98). This is close, though it may be said it is distant, since the exegetes agree on the first meaning.

His words, ﴿Show me﴾, replace ﴿Have you considered﴾, because both convey the meaning "inform me." It may also be said that His words, ﴿Have you considered﴾, are a genuine interrogative, and ﴿Show me﴾ is a command of challenge for clarification. So when He said ﴿Have you considered﴾, meaning: Do you know these you invoke as they are, and in the state of helplessness they are in? Or do you imagine in them some power? If you know them to be powerless, how do you worship them? And if it occurred to you that they have some power, then show me their power, in what it lies: is it in the earth, as some have said, "Allah is the god of the heavens, and these are the gods of the earth"? These are the ones who said, "The affairs of the earth are from the stars and the idols whose forms they are." Or is it in the heavens? As some have said, "The heaven was created with the help of the angels, and the angels are partners in the creation of the heavens, and these idols are their forms." Or is their power in intercession for you? As some have said, "The angels created nothing, but they are close to Allah, so we worship them that they may intercede for us." Then do they have a book from Allah in which there is His permission for them to intercede?

His words, ﴿Or have We given them a book﴾: regarding the pronoun returning to it, there are two possibilities:

The first: it returns to the partners, meaning: Have We given the partners a book?

The second: it returns to the polytheists, meaning: Have We given the polytheists a book? On the first, its meaning is what we have mentioned: Is there with what has been made a partner a book from Allah in which it is stated that it has intercession with Allah? For no one intercedes with Him except by His permission. On the second, its meaning is that the worship of these people is either by reason, and there is no reason in one who worships what has not created a single part of the earth nor anything in the heavens; or by transmission (naql), and We have not given the polytheists a book in which We command them to prostrate to these. Even if We had commanded it, it would be permissible, as We commanded prostration to Adam and facing the direction of the Ka'bah. So this worship is neither rational nor transmitted. Thus the promise some of them make to one another is nothing but delusion, which Satan deceived them with and beautified for them the worship of idols.

Then, when He had made clear that the idols have no creation and no power, nor any power over a single part, He showed that Allah is capable, by His words: ﴿Indeed, Allah holds the heavens and the earth lest they cease; and if they should cease, no one could hold them after Him. Indeed, He is ever Forbearing and Forgiving﴾. It may also be said: when He had made clear their association, He stated that the consequence of their association is the cessation of the heavens and the earth, as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿The heavens are about to burst apart from it, and the earth splits open, and the mountains collapse in ruin, that they attribute to the Most Merciful a son﴾ (Maryam: 90). This is indicated by His words at the end of the verse: ﴿Indeed, He is ever Forbearing and Forgiving﴾. "He is Forbearing" means He did not abandon punishing them except out of His forbearance; otherwise they would deserve the falling of the sky and the crushing of the earth upon them. He delayed the removal of the heavens until the Hour arrives, out of forbearance.

The verse may also bear a third meaning: that it is by way of concession (taslim), and establishing the sought matter on the assumption of concession as well, as if He, Exalted, said: "Your partners did not create anything from the earth, nor a part in the heavens, nor were they able to intercede; so there is no worship for them. Suppose they did do something of the things; can they hold the heavens and the earth? It is impossible for them to claim they have this power, because they did not claim it themselves, as Allah, the Exalted, said about them: ﴿And if you asked them who created the heavens and the earth, they would surely say, "Allah"﴾ (Luqman: 25). This is confirmed by His words: ﴿And if they should cease, no one could hold them after Him﴾. Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And they swore by Allah their most solemn oaths that if a warner came to them, they would surely be better guided than any of the (other) nations. But when a warner came to them, it increased them only in aversion, (43) out of arrogance in the land and evil scheming. But evil scheming does not encompass anyone except its own people.﴾

When He had explained their denial of monotheism (tawhid), He mentioned their denial of the Messenger and their exaggeration in it. They used to swear that they would not deny the messengers if it became clear to them that they were messengers. They said: "We only deny Muhammad (ﷺ) because he is a liar. If it became clear to us that he is a messenger, we would believe," as Allah the Exalted said about them: ﴿And they swore by Allah their most solemn oaths that if a sign came to them, they would surely believe in it﴾ (al-An'am: 109). This is an exaggeration on their part in denial, just as one who denies a person's debt may say: "By Allah, if I knew that I owed him anything, I would have paid it and added to it," to show that the claimant is demanding something false. Likewise, here they were obstinate and said: "By Allah, if a messenger came to us, we would be the best guided of the nations." But when a warner, i.e., Muhammad (ﷺ), came to them, that is, when his coming to them was established with clear proof, it increased them only in aversion. Before the prophethood they were disbelievers in Allah, and after it they became disbelievers in Allah and His Messenger. Also, before the prophethood they were not punished as they were after the prophethood.

Some exegetes (mufassirun) said: The people of Makkah used to reproach the Jews and Christians for having denied their messengers when they came to them, and they said: "If a messenger came to us, we would obey him and follow him." There is a difficulty here, since the polytheists denied prophethood and resurrection absolutely. So how could they acknowledge the messengers? From where did they know that the Jews had denied, when no scripture had come to them? And had it not been for the Book of Allah and the explanation of His Messenger, from where would the polytheists have known that they affirmed some things and denied others? Rather, what is meant is what we mentioned: they used to say, "We would not deny a messenger if one came to us; we only deny that Muhammad is a messenger, on the grounds that he is a liar. If his being a messenger were established, we would believe."

His saying ﴿when he came to them﴾ means: when his coming with the miracle was established for them. In His saying ﴿better guided﴾ there are two interpretations:

The first: The meaning is "better guided than what we are upon." On this view, His saying ﴿than any of the (other) nations﴾ is explanatory (lil-tabyin), as one says: "Zayd is one of the Muslims." This is supported by His saying the Exalted: ﴿But when a warner came to them, it increased them only in aversion﴾, meaning they became more astray than they had been, while they had been saying: "We would be better guided."

The second: The meaning is "that we would be better guided than one of the nations," as one says: "Zayd is more deserving than Amr."

Regarding "the nations" there are two interpretations:

The first: The meaning is generality, i.e., better guided than any of the nations, and this contains an implicit allusion (ta'rid).

The second: The meaning is definite reference (ta'rif al-'ahd), i.e., the nation of Muhammad, Musa and Isa, and those who were in their times.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿out of arrogance in the land﴾. Its accusative form (nasb) admits three possibilities:

One: It is a circumstantial state (hal), i.e., "being arrogant in the land."

His saying ﴿and evil scheming﴾ is a genitive of genus (idafat al-jins) to its type, as one says "ʿilm al-fiqh" (the science of jurisprudence) and "hirfat al-haddadah" (the craft of smithing). Its verification is that one says: its meaning is "they schemed a wicked scheme," then it was made definite (ʿuruffa) because their scheming was evident, then the definite article was dropped and it was made a genitive to "the evil," because evil is the most evident of matters. It is also possible to say that scheming (makr) is used in the sense of action, as we mentioned in His saying the Exalted: ﴿And those who plot evil deeds﴾ (Fatir: 10), i.e., those who do evil deeds. Their "evil scheming" is everything that proceeded from them of intent to harm, preventing people from entering faith, and openly displaying denial. Then He said: ﴿But evil scheming does not encompass anyone except its own people﴾, i.e., it does not surround anyone except its doer.

In His saying ﴿does not encompass﴾ and His saying ﴿except its own people﴾ there are benefits:

As for His saying ﴿encompass﴾, it indicates encompassment, which is more than mere reaching, and it contains a warning that is absent in saying "does not reach" or "does not arrive." As for His saying ﴿its own people﴾, it contains what is absent in the statement "evil scheming does not encompass anyone except the schemer," so that the evildoer will not feel secure, for one who does evil whose scheming is evil may be overtaken by another evil as recompense for an evil deed. But if he is not evil, he is not one of its people, and so he is safe from evil scheming. As for negation and affirmation, the benefit is restriction (hasr), unlike the statement "evil scheming returns upon its people," which does not indicate that it does not return upon anyone else. If someone says: "We often see that the schemer schemes, the scheming benefits him, and he overcomes his opponent through scheming, while the verse indicates that this does not happen?" We reply: the answer to this is in several respects:

First: The scheming mentioned in the verse is the scheming they plotted against the Prophet (ﷺ) by resolving to kill and expel him, and it did not befall anyone except them, since they were killed on the day of Badr and elsewhere.

Second: We say that "evil scheming" is general, and this is the more correct view, for the Prophet, peace be upon him, forbade scheming, and it was reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Do not practise scheming, nor assist one who practises scheming, for Allah says: ﴿But evil scheming does not encompass anyone except its own people﴾."

On this view, that person against whom scheming is directed is not one of its people, so it is not an objection (naqd) to the argument.

Third: Matters are judged by their outcomes. Whoever is schemed against by another and the scheming takes effect on him quickly, in outward appearance, in reality he is the successful one, and the schemer is the one who perishes. This is like the ease of the disbeliever and the hardship of the believer in this world. This meaning is clarified by His saying the Exalted: ﴿Then do they await anything but the way of the former peoples?﴾ That is: if their scheming has currency in the present, the outcome belongs to piety, and matters are judged by their conclusions, so they will perish as the former ones perished.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 35, verse 43:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then do they await anything but the way (sunnah) of the former peoples?﴾ That is, after this there remains for them nothing but waiting for destruction, and that is the way of the former peoples. And concerning this there are several issues:

The first issue: Destruction is not "the way of the former peoples"; rather it is "the way of God with the former peoples." We say: the answer to this is from two aspects.

The first: The verbal noun (al-masdar), which is the absolute object (al-maf'ul al-mutlaq), may be attributed to the agent and to the object, because it is connected to both of them in one respect but not in another. It is said, when Zayd struck ʿAmr: "I marvel at the striking of ʿAmr, how he was struck despite his resolve and strength," and "I marvel at the striking of Zayd, how he struck despite his knowledge and wisdom." Likewise, the way of God with them: He attributed it to them, because it is a way that was established with them; and He attributed it to Himself afterwards by His saying: ﴿So you will not find any alteration in the way of God﴾, because it is one of the ways of God. Once you know this, we say: He attributed it at first to them when He said: ﴿the way of the former peoples﴾, because the way of God is destruction for associating partners and honour for submission to Islam, so it was not known whether they were awaiting one or the other; when He said "the way of the former peoples," it was distinguished. In the second instance He attributed it to God, because once it was known, attributing it to God is its exaltation, and it became clear that it is a matter that is certain to occur, and that there is no repeller of it.

The second: The intended meaning of "the way of the former peoples" is their persistence in denial and their arrogance in refusing to acknowledge, while the way of God is their extermination because of their insistence. It is as if He said: "You want to bring about the way of the former peoples, while God brings about a way for which there is no alteration, and no turning away from its deserving object."

The second issue: Alteration (tabdil) is a change (tahwil); so what is the wisdom in the repetition? We say: By His saying ﴿So you will not find any alteration in the way of God﴾ it is known that the punishment has no substitution by anything else; and by His saying ﴿nor will you find any transformation in the way of God﴾ it is known that the punishment, although it has no substitution by reward, does not turn away from its deserving object to another, and thus the threat to the evildoer is complete.

The third issue: The addressee in His saying ﴿So you will not find﴾ may bear two aspects, and this has been mentioned repeatedly before:

The first: that it is general, as if He said: "So you will not find, O listener, any alteration in the way of God."

The second: that it is directed to Muhammad ﷺ. On this view, it is as if He said: "The way of God is that He does not destroy the remaining people among whom is one whose faith God has decreed; so when one whom God knows will believe, believes, He destroys the rest," as Noah said: ﴿Indeed, if You leave them﴾ (Nuh: 27), that is, "You delay the matter, and the time of Your way has come."

Then He said, exalted is He: ﴿Have they not travelled through the earth and seen how was the end of those before them, who were greater than them in strength?﴾

When He mentioned that the earlier peoples had a established way (sunnah), which is destruction, He alerted them by reminding them of the condition of the earlier peoples. For they used to pass by their dwellings and see their traces, and their hope was beyond their hope, and their deeds were less than their deeds. As for the first, it was due to the length of their lives and the intensity of their power. As for their deeds, it was because they did not deny the likes of Muhammad, nor Muhammad himself, whereas you, O people of Makkah, have denied Muhammad and those who came before him. As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and they were greater than them in strength﴾, we have mentioned it in Surat al-Rum, and there remain some discussions concerning it:

The first: He said there, ﴿they were greater﴾ without a waw, and here He said it with a waw, so what is the difference? We say: the saying of the speaker, "Have you not seen Zayd, how he honoured me, and he is greater than you," indicates that the speaker is informing him that Zayd is greater. But if he says, "Have you not seen him, how he honoured me, he is greater than you," it indicates that it has been established that both meanings are present for the listener, as if he saw that he honoured him, and saw that he was greater than him. There is no doubt that this latter expression indicates that the second matter is as evident as the first, such that it does not need the speaker to inform or announce it. Knowing this, we say: what is mentioned here is only their being greater than them in strength, and perhaps this was evident to them, so He said it with a waw, meaning: your seeing what befell the outcome of their affair falls upon their strength as well. Whereas there, many things are mentioned, for He said: ﴿they were greater than them in strength and they tilled the earth and cultivated it﴾ (al-Rum: 9). And in another place He said: ﴿Have they not travelled through the earth and seen how was the end of those before them? They were more numerous than them, and greater in strength and in traces upon the earth﴾ (Ghafir: 82). Perhaps their knowledge was not attained

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah is not to be frustrated by anything in the heavens or on the earth; indeed He is ever Knowing, Competent﴾, it admits of two aspects:

One of them: that it is an explanation for them, meaning that the earlier peoples, despite the intensity of their power, did not frustrate Allah nor escape Him, so they are more deserving not to frustrate Him.

The second: that it is a cutting off of the hopes of the ignorant, for if someone were to say, "Suppose the earlier peoples were stronger and had longer lives, we will still extract by our cleverness what exceeds their powers, and we will seek help from earthly things that have properties, or heavenly stars that have effects," then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And Allah is not to be frustrated by anything in the heavens or on the earth; indeed He is ever Knowing﴾ of their deeds and their words, ﴿Competent﴾ to destroy them and uproot them.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿If God were to take people to task for what they have earned, He would not leave on its back a single creature, but He defers them to a specified term. And when their term comes, indeed God is ever Seeing of His servants.﴾

When God had warned the deniers with the example of those who came before them, and they, because of their intense obstinacy and corrupt beliefs, were hastening the punishment and saying, "Hasten for us our punishment," God said: the punishment has a term, and God does not take people to task for the mere fact of wrongdoing, for man is indeed wrongdoing and ignorant. He takes them to task only when they persist and when people have despaired of their faith, while there are still those among them whom God has decreed to believe. So when no one among them remains who would believe, He destroys the deniers. Had He taken them to task for the mere fact of wrongdoing, there would have been a destruction every day. In this verse there are several issues:

**First issue:** If God takes people to task for what they have earned, why do the animals perish too? We say the answer has several aspects.

The first: the creation of animals is a blessing. When people disbelieve, God removes the blessings, and animals are among the closest of blessings, since the simple comes before the compound. The compound is either mineral, or growing (living). The growing is either animal or plant. The animal is either human or non-human. Thus animals are, in the world of the elements, the highest rank of created things after humans.

The second: this is an illustration of the severity and comprehensiveness of the punishment. The survival of things depends on humans, just as the survival of humans depends on things. Humans manage and improve things, so things persist, and then humans benefit from them. If the destruction were general, no human would remain to cultivate, so buildings and crops would not remain, nor would domestic animals, since their survival depends on humans protecting them from loss and destruction by providing water and fodder.

The third: the sending down of rain is a favor from God toward His servants. If they do not deserve the favor, the rains are cut off from them, drought appears on the face of the earth, and all living creatures die. This is God's saying: ﴿He would not leave on its back a single creature﴾.

The third aspect (another version): because when the rains are cut off, land animals die, while sea animals live on the water of the seas.

**Second issue:** God's saying ﴿on its back﴾ is a kinayah (metonymy) for the earth, though the earth is not mentioned. How is it known? We say: from what came before and what comes after. As for what came before, it is His saying: ﴿Nothing in the heavens or on the earth can ever frustrate Him﴾, which is the nearest of the mentioned things suitable for the pronoun to refer back to. As for what comes after, it is His saying: ﴿a single creature﴾, since creatures are on the back of the earth. If it is said: how can the surface on which creatures live be called both "the face of the earth" and "the back of the earth," when the face is opposite to the back, like opposites? We say: insofar as the earth is like a beast carrying loads, and carrying is done on the back, it is called "the back of the earth." And insofar as that surface faces the creatures and confronts them, it is called "its face." Moreover, the back is opposite the belly, and "back" (ẓahr) and "apparent" (ẓāhir) are from the same root, while "belly" (baṭn) and "hidden" (bāṭin) are from the same root. So the face of the earth is called "back" because it is the apparent part, while the rest of it is hidden and belly.

**Third issue:** In His saying ﴿but He defers them to a specified term﴾ there are several aspects:

The first: until the Day of Resurrection, which is the specified term mentioned in many places.

The second: the day when no one among the creation who will believe is found, as explained above.

The third: for every nation there is a term, and for every term there is a Book. The term of the people of Muhammad (ﷺ) is the days of killing and captivity, like the day of Badr and others.

**Fourth issue:** His saying ﴿And when their term comes, indeed God is ever Seeing of His servants﴾ is a consolation for the believers. This is because when He said ﴿He would not leave on its back a single creature﴾ and said ﴿And beware of a trial which will not afflict only those of you who have done wrong﴾ (al-Anfal: 25), He then said: when the destruction comes, God is Seeing of His servants. He either saves them, or their death is a drawing near to God, not a punishment. It may be said: you have stated that God does not take people to task for the mere fact of wrongdoing, but only when people gather in error. And we say that when He destroys, He destroys the believer too, so how is this? We say: we have stated that if death and annihilation are for punishment, it is a taking to task for sin and a destruction; but if it is to bring reward, it is neither destruction nor taking to task. God takes people to task only when disbelief is widespread. As for His saying "Seeing" (baṣīr), the word is more complete in consolation than "Knowing" (ʿalīm) and others, because one who sees a thing and looks at it is more deserving of saving it than one who knows its condition without seeing it. And God knows best.
